t: Vodouists serve Bondye, a remote creator God, through the lwa, spirits mostly named after West and Central African deities, equated with Catholic saints and grouped in nations such as the Rada and the Petwo.
In the dans, the night ceremony of drumming, song and dance, a lwa is invited to possess a worshipper, the chwal or “horse”, and to speak through them to the congregation.

Forbidden in the colony, Vodou became Haiti’s dominant religion after the Revolution; long maligned by outsiders as sorcery, it was officially recognised in 2003 and has spread with Haitian emigrants.
dyk: The word Vodou comes from the Fon language of West Africa: Vôdoun, a word for a spirit or deity in the kingdom of Dahomey, was first recorded in the Doctrina Christiana of 1658.
ev: Spanish colonists on Hispaniola begin importing enslaved West Africans, some of them priests of African traditional religions
The French Code Noir forbids the open practice of African religions and orders that the enslaved be baptised as Roman Catholics
Among the enslaved of Saint-Domingue, African religions mixed with Catholic and Freemasonic elements take the form of Vodou
According to legend, a Vodou ritual at Bois-Caïman sparks the Haitian Revolution
The Roman Catholic Church cuts ties with Haiti until 1860, and Vodou becomes the country’s dominant religion
The United States occupies Haiti until 1934, stirring foreign interest in Vodou and its reassessment by Haitian indigenists
The government launches Operation Nettoyage, a Church-backed campaign to destroy many Vodou temples
President Jean-Bertrand Aristide grants Vodou official recognition, after the constitution of 1987 enshrined freedom of religion

f.origin: Hispaniola, in the French colony of Saint-Domingue that became Haiti, between the 16th and 19th centuries, among enslaved West and Central Africans, especially Fon and Bakongo; it took the form of Vodou around the mid-18th century.
f.founder: none: it arose from the blending of several West and Central African traditional religions with Roman Catholicism and Freemasonry, and has no central authority or single leader.
f.scriptures: none written: its teachings pass on orally and through ritual, song and the langaj of the rites, though many practitioners have used texts since these appeared in the mid-20th century.
f.followers: Never counted, as Haiti has had no accurate census; in 1992 Leslie Desmangles put the Haitian practitioners at six million. Most Haitians practise both Vodou and Catholicism, and communities live in the United States, Cuba and elsewhere.
